title: THE WOMEN NOBODY ASKED
paragraphs:
THE WOMEN NOBODY ASKED
What Bilhah, Zilpah, Rizpah, and Hagar Reveal About Women With Less Power—and the God Who Still Saw Them
There are women in the Bible whose stories make us uncomfortable because Scripture refuses to clean the blood off the floor before inviting us into the room.
Bilhah.
Zilpah.
Rizpah.
Hagar.
Their names are easy to read past.
Their lives are not.

They lived in worlds where other people frequently possessed more social, economic, familial, or political power than they did. Decisions involving their bodies, children, homes, futures, and security could be made by people standing above them.
And here is what makes their stories especially disturbing:
Sometimes the people with greater power were themselves wounded people.
Rachel was suffering.
Leah was suffering.
Sarah was suffering.
David was carrying the responsibility of a kingdom suffering under famine.
Pain was everywhere.
But pain does not automatically make everything we do with power righteous.
Sometimes wounded people wound people with less power.
Sometimes somebody else's desperation becomes your captivity.
Sometimes you become the solution to a problem you never created.
And perhaps that sentence already feels too personal.
Because maybe you know what it is like to have somebody else's expectations placed on your shoulders.
Maybe you were the child who had to keep the family peaceful.
The wife expected to absorb everything quietly.
The employee who could not afford to say no.
The woman whose usefulness seemed more important than her heart.
The person everyone needed—but nobody really asked, “How are you?”
Maybe people discussed your future while you sat in the room.
Maybe they decided what was “best” for you without ever asking what happened inside you afterward.
If so, do not rush through these women.
Sit beside them.
Because the Bible does something extraordinary with people the powerful world might have treated as background characters.
It remembers their names.
And ultimately, their stories lead us toward Jesus Christ—the King who did not use His authority to consume the vulnerable, but gave Himself to save sinners.
Start with Bilhah.
Rachel is devastated by infertility. Genesis 30 opens with Rachel envying Leah and crying to Jacob for children.
Then she says something that can sound almost ordinary after centuries of familiarity with the story:
“Here is my maid Bilhah.”
The Hebrew is sharper when we allow ourselves to hear the social relationship being described:

הִנֵּה אֲמָתִי בִלְהָה
hinneh ʾamati Bilhah
“Here is my female servant, Bilhah.”
Rachel continues:

בֹּא אֵלֶיהָ וְתֵלֵד עַל־בִּרְכַּי
bo ʾeleha wetēled ʿal-birkay
“Go in to her, and she shall bear upon my knees.”
Genesis then says Rachel gave Bilhah to Jacob as a wife, and Bilhah conceived and bore him a son.
Stop there.

Do not import twenty-first-century assumptions carelessly into an ancient household. Surrogacy-like arrangements involving enslaved or servant women existed within the ancient world, and Scripture is describing a household vastly different from ours.
But neither should we make the opposite mistake.
Description is not endorsement.
The Bible can faithfully tell us what human beings did without declaring everything they did morally ideal.
And what is striking in Genesis 30 is whose voices dominate the naming of Bilhah's children.
Bilhah carries Dan.
Rachel names him.
Bilhah carries Naphtali.
Rachel names him.
Rachel interprets the pregnancies through Rachel's struggle with Leah.
Bilhah's womb becomes part of another woman's rivalry.
Read that again slowly.
A woman can be hurting deeply and still possess power over somebody more vulnerable than herself.
That is one of the uncomfortable truths these stories force Christians to confront.
Victimhood in one relationship does not guarantee righteousness in another.
Rachel knows the agony of infertility.
But Bilhah still occupies the weaker social position.
Then Leah enters the same pattern.
When Leah stops bearing children, Genesis says:

וַתִּקַּח אֶת־זִלְפָּה שִׁפְחָתָהּ
vattiqqaḥ ʾet-Zilpah shifḥatah
“She took Zilpah her female servant.”
Leah gives Zilpah to Jacob as a wife.
Zilpah bears Gad.
Then Asher.
Again, the children speak loudly in the story.
The mother barely speaks at all.
Rachel speaks.
Leah speaks.
Jacob appears.
Children are named.
The household grows.
Israel's tribal history advances.
And Bilhah and Zilpah almost disappear behind what their bodies produced.
Yet they did not disappear from God's story.
Dan mattered.
Naphtali mattered.
Gad mattered.
Asher mattered.
Four tribes of Israel came through women whose own recorded speech is strikingly absent from these birth narratives.
That should make us careful whenever we confuse silence with insignificance.

The Bible does not give us permission to invent Bilhah's or Zilpah's inner thoughts. We should not manufacture trauma Scripture does not explicitly describe, pretend we know every detail of their consent, or force modern psychological categories onto an ancient text.
But the text gives us enough to recognize an unequal social arrangement.
Their comparative lack of recorded voice does not mean they lacked personhood before God.
And somebody reading this needs that distinction.
Because perhaps people know what you produced but not what producing it cost you.
They remember the meal.
Not the exhaustion.
They remember the children you raised.
Not the nights you cried.
They remember the ministry you helped build.
Not the moment somebody used “God's will” to pressure you into silence.
They remember what you gave.
They never asked what was taken.
And somewhere inside you is a dangerous question you have been afraid to ask:
Did God see what nobody else noticed?
Hagar answers.
Hagar is perhaps one of Scripture's clearest portraits of a woman living beneath the power of others.
Sarah is barren.
The promise seems delayed.
Years pass.
Hope hurts.
So Sarah gives her Egyptian servant Hagar to Abraham.
Again, we should read the ancient account honestly.
Hagar is not introduced as a socially equal woman entering negotiations from an equal position.
She is Sarah's Egyptian servant.
Then she becomes pregnant.
Conflict erupts.
Sarah complains to Abraham.
Abraham tells Sarah that Hagar is in her hand.
Sarah treats her harshly.
The Hebrew verb describing Sarah's treatment is built from the root ענה, ʿ-n-h, associated here with affliction or harsh treatment.
And Hagar runs.
A pregnant foreign servant woman flees into the wilderness.
No powerful relatives are mentioned coming to retrieve her.
No wealth protects her.
No institution intervenes.
But Someone finds her.
The messenger of the LORD meets Hagar by a spring.
And then Scripture records words that should shake anyone who has ever believed God only notices important people:

כִּי־שָׁמַע יְהוָה אֶל־עָנְיֵךְ
ki-shama YHWH ʾel-ʿonyekh
“For the LORD has heard your affliction.”
Her son's name, Ishmael—יִשְׁמָעֵאל, Yishmaʿel—is tied to this declaration that God hears.
The woman who could be ordered around by human beings discovers that heaven has been listening.
Then Hagar does something extraordinary.
She speaks of the God who spoke to her as:

אַתָּה אֵל רֳאִי
ʾattah ʾEl Roʾi
“You are El-roi”—commonly understood along the lines of “God of seeing,” though the exact wording of the surrounding Hebrew is difficult and translations vary.
Do not miss the wonder.
Hagar had been looked at as a servant.
Looked at as a solution.
Looked at as a reproductive answer.
Looked at as a problem when household conflict erupted.
But in the wilderness she discovers what it means to be seen by God.
Not used.
Seen.
Not merely evaluated.
Seen.
Not reduced to what she can provide.
Seen.
And perhaps that is where this article found you.
You have spent years being useful.
Useful to your family.
Useful to your church.
Useful to your spouse.
Useful to your employer.
Useful to everyone.
And secretly you have wondered whether anybody would still love you if you stopped producing.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not announce that your value comes from your usefulness.
Your deepest problem is not merely that other people have failed to see you. Like every descendant of Adam, you are a sinner who needs reconciliation with a holy God.
And this is where Christianity offers something infinitely greater than self-esteem.
God sees you completely—including the parts you desperately hope nobody sees.
Your wounds.
Your resentment.
Your hidden sins.
Your bitterness.
Your compromises.
Your fear.
Your secret hunger to be loved.
Nothing is hidden.
And still the Gospel says Christ came for sinners.
That is grace.
Not God pretending your sin is harmless.
Not God calling evil good.
Grace is God confronting sin so completely that the Son of God goes to the cross to deal with it.
Hagar encounters the God who sees.
But centuries later, in Jesus Christ, we discover just how far the God who sees is willing to go to save.
Before we reach Calvary, however, there is another woman sitting on a rock.
Her name is Rizpah.
And her story may be one of the most agonizing scenes in the Old Testament.
Rizpah was a concubine of Saul.
Her social position was connected to royal power without giving her the power of the king.
Then comes 2 Samuel 21.

Israel is suffering famine. The narrative connects the crisis to Saul's bloodguilt against the Gibeonites. David asks the Gibeonites what restitution they require. They request seven male descendants of Saul.
Among those handed over are Rizpah's two sons, Armoni and Mephibosheth.
They die.
And then their mother does something almost unbearable to imagine.
וַתִּקַּח רִצְפָּה בַת־אַיָּה אֶת־הַשַּׂק
“Rizpah daughter of Aiah took sackcloth.”
She spreads it for herself on a rock.
And she stays.
From the beginning of harvest until rain comes.
By day she keeps the birds away.
By night she keeps the wild animals away.
She cannot reverse what happened.
She cannot command an army.
She cannot issue a royal decree.
She cannot restore breath to her sons.
But she can stay.
So she stays.
Imagine the nights.
The smell.
The grief.
The exhaustion.
The sound of wings.
The movement in the darkness.
A grieving mother with almost no political power refuses to abandon the bodies of her children.
Then one of the most quietly explosive sentences in the narrative appears:

וַיֻּגַּד לְדָוִד
vayyuggad leDavid
“And it was told David…”
The king hears what Rizpah has done.
Her vigil reaches the throne.
David then acts to gather the bones of Saul and Jonathan, as well as those who had been executed, and provides burial.
Rizpah did not command the king.
Her faithfulness became impossible for the king to ignore.
There is something sacred in that.
Not because grief always changes earthly authorities.
It does not.
Not because every faithful protest receives justice before sunset.
It does not.
But because Scripture refuses to treat this grieving concubine as scenery.
It records her name.
Her sackcloth.
Her rock.
Her endurance.
Her defense of the dead.
Her action reaches David's ears.
And her story has survived thousands of years.
Somebody needs to hear this:
Powerlessness is not the same thing as worthlessness.
Bilhah had less power.
Zilpah had less power.
Hagar had less power.
Rizpah had less power.
But none of them was invisible to the biblical story.
And now we have to ask the uncomfortable question.
What do these women reveal about us?
Not merely about “society.”
Us.
Christians.
Families.
Churches.
Marriages.
Ministries.
Employers.
Parents.
Leaders.
Anyone who has power over somebody else.
Because almost everybody is Bilhah somewhere and Rachel somewhere else.
Almost everybody knows what it means to lack power in one room while possessing it in another.
You can be mistreated by your boss and harsh toward your children.
Ignored by your husband and cruel toward the waitress.
Disrespected by church leadership and controlling toward the volunteer beneath you.
Marginalized in one relationship and manipulative in another.
That is why these stories cannot merely become weapons we point outward.
The Gospel turns the mirror toward us.
How do you treat people who cannot advance your career?
How do you speak to people who cannot punish you?
How do you treat the person serving your food?
The cleaner?
The employee who needs the job?
The child who cannot leave?
The elderly parent who now depends on you?
The spouse who trusted you with vulnerabilities nobody else knows?
The church member nobody considers influential?
The struggling believer who has nothing impressive to offer your ministry?
Your theology of human dignity is revealed most clearly by how you treat people whose approval you do not need.
And then Jesus enters the picture.
Not merely as an inspirational example.
As Lord.
As Redeemer.
As the crucified and risen King.
Jesus possessed authority unlike anyone else.
Yet listen to how He described His mission in Mark 10:45:
Καὶ γὰρ ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου οὐκ ἦλθεν διακονηθῆναι, ἀλλὰ διακονῆσαι…
“For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve…”
And then:
καὶ δοῦναι τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ λύτρον ἀντὶ πολλῶν
“…and to give His life as a ransom for many.”
The Greek word λύτρον—lytron—means a ransom, the price associated with release.
Look at the difference.
Sinful human power says:
“What can you give me?”
Jesus says:
“I give My life.”
Sinful power consumes.
Jesus serves.
Sinful power sacrifices the vulnerable to preserve itself.
Jesus, though innocent, willingly gives Himself for guilty sinners.
Sinful power asks who is beneath me.
Jesus kneels.
Touches lepers.
Receives children.
Speaks with socially despised people.
Responds to beggars.
Honors women as disciples and witnesses.
Calls sinners to repentance.
And then walks toward a cross.
This is why Christianity cannot reduce the answer to vulnerable women—or vulnerable men—to vague empowerment slogans.
Our hope is deeper.
Our hope has nail scars.
The answer is Jesus Christ.
The One with all authority willingly humbled Himself.
The sinless One died for sinners.
The rejected Stone became the cornerstone.
The crucified Christ rose.
And in Him, people whom human societies separate by ethnicity, status, and sex stand equally dependent upon grace.
Paul writes:
οὐκ ἔνι Ἰουδαῖος οὐδὲ Ἕλλην, οὐκ ἔνι δοῦλος οὐδὲ ἐλεύθερος, οὐκ ἔνι ἄρσεν καὶ θῆλυ· πάντες γὰρ ὑμεῖς εἷς ἐστε ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ.
“There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is neither male and female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus.”
Paul is not claiming earthly distinctions magically cease to exist.
He is declaring something glorious about standing in Christ.
Slave and free come to Christ needing the same grace.
Male and female come needing the same Savior.
Jew and Gentile enter the family of God through Christ.
No human being reaches the foot of the cross carrying a VIP pass.
And no repentant sinner kneeling there is second-class.
That means the Church must never baptize domination simply because domination happens to benefit the powerful.
Neither can we twist stories like Hagar's, Bilhah's, Zilpah's, or Rizpah's into claims Scripture itself never makes.
Faithfulness means refusing both errors.
We do not sanitize the text.
And we do not rewrite it.
We let Scripture disturb us where Scripture is disturbing.
We let it correct us where we have confused cultural power with God's character.
And then we look to Christ.
Maybe you came into this article thinking about women who had less power.
But perhaps somewhere along the way you realized the Holy Spirit was asking about what you do with yours.
That realization matters.
Because repentance begins when excuses stop.
Maybe you need to repent for using someone's dependence against them.
Maybe you have controlled with money.
Manipulated with Scripture.
Demanded silence in the name of “submission.”
Used your position in ministry to make questioning you feel like questioning God.
Perhaps you made somebody's vulnerability expensive.
Perhaps you treated another person's forgiveness as permission to keep hurting them.
Or perhaps you are on the other side.
You are the one who was controlled.
And you have carried shame for years because somebody convinced you that what happened proved something was wrong with you.
Listen carefully.
Another person's sin against you does not become righteous because they possessed authority.
And being sinned against does not remove your own need for Christ either.
The Gospel gives us something more beautiful than competing claims of innocence.
At the cross, victims can bring wounds that God does not minimize.
Sinners can bring guilt God does not excuse.
The abused do not have to call evil good.
The guilty do not have to pretend they never sinned.
Both are summoned into the light.
There, justice matters.
Truth matters.
Repentance matters.
Forgiveness matters.
Grace matters.
And Jesus remains Lord.
Maybe your prayer tonight is not eloquent.
Maybe it is only:
“Jesus, You see me.”
That is enough to begin speaking honestly.
Or perhaps:
“Jesus, forgive me for how I have used power.”
Do not run from that conviction.
Run to Christ.
Repentance is not God destroying the repentant sinner.
It is grace dragging what was killing you into the light.
Christ did not die so we could become better at hiding.
He died and rose to make sinners new.
You can simply write, “Jesus, forgive me.”
If you are exhausted from fighting quietly, comment, “Pray for me.”
If God has been healing places nobody else knows about, write, “Christ is still healing me.”
And if you have spent years pretending everything is fine when it isn't, perhaps today is the day to say, “No more hiding.”
Not because a comment saves you.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes bringing one honest sentence into the light is how we stop rehearsing the lie that nobody else understands.
Someone reading beneath you may discover they are not alone.
And somebody on your Facebook friends list may need this truth more than you realize.
But supporting faithful Gospel work can be one practical expression of generosity, partnership, and a desire to help biblical teaching reach another person.
And beyond the products, there is something we care about far more.
Discipleship.
Not because every sentence is perfect, but because there may come a day when you forget again that human power and divine worth are not the same thing.
Share it with the woman who has spent her life feeling like Bilhah—needed but rarely heard.
Send it to the grieving mother who understands something of Rizpah's rock.
Send it to the leader who needs to remember that authority in the kingdom of Christ is never permission to consume people.
Send it to the man who wants to become more like Jesus in the way he treats women, children, employees, strangers, and everyone who possesses less power than he does.
But before you leave, remember the four women.
Bilhah.
Zilpah.
Hagar.
Rizpah.
One bore children while another woman spoke their names.
One bore children while another woman celebrated.
One ran into a wilderness and discovered that God had heard her affliction.
One sat beneath the dead until her grief reached the ears of a king.
Different women.
Different stories.
Different wounds.
But together they whisper a warning to anyone with power:
Be careful what you do with people who cannot easily say no to you.
And they whisper hope to anyone who feels powerless:
Human beings may overlook you without heaven losing sight of you.
But there is one final truth even greater than being seen.
The God who sees did not remain distant.
Jesus came.
Jesus served.
Jesus touched the rejected.
Jesus called sinners to repentance.
Jesus carried the cross.
Jesus gave His life as a ransom.
Jesus rose from the grave.
And Jesus still receives repentant sinners.
So bring Him the part of your story nobody wanted to hear.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the anger.
Bring Him the memories.
Bring Him your own sins too.
Bring Him what people did to you.
Bring Him what you did to others.
Bring Him the wilderness.
Bring Him the rock.
Bring Him the years when you felt useful but unloved.
Bring Him the nights when nobody came.
Because grace does not mean the scandal never happened.
Grace means the scandal does not get the final word.

You may have been treated like a footnote in someone else's story, but beneath the eyes of Christ, you were never invisible—and at His cross, even the darkest chapter can become the place where grace begins writing again.
